questions.explanation: Land is natural resources, labor is human effort, physical capital is produced tools and equipment, and entrepreneurship organizes the others and bears risk.

questions.explanation: Market economies rely on prices and private decisions; command economies on central planning; mixed economies combine markets with government roles.

options.text: Price will increase; quantity will increase

options.text: Price will decrease; quantity will increase
options.why: Not this one: Price will increase, and quantity will decrease.

options.text: Price will decrease; quantity will decrease
options.why: Not this one: Price will increase.

questions.explanation: Fewer oranges raise input costs, decreasing supply: supply decreases. A supply shift moves price and quantity in opposite directions.

questions.stem: At the world price of 4, domestic consumers buy 85 units and domestic producers supply 54. A tariff of 1 raises the domestic price to 5, where consumers buy 75 and producers supply 64. By how much do imports fall?

options.why: This is the level of imports after the tariff.
This is only the fall in consumption; domestic production also rises.
This is the level of imports before the tariff.
Correct. Imports fall from 31 to 11.

questions.explanation: Imports = domestic quantity demanded − domestic quantity supplied: 31 before, 11 after, a fall of 20.

questions.stem: A firm lowers its price and finds that its total revenue decreases. Over this range, demand for its product is

options.text: perfectly elastic
options.why: With perfectly elastic demand, any price increase would lose all sales.

options.text: unit elastic
options.why: With unit elastic demand, total revenue would not change.

options.text: price elastic
options.why: Use the total revenue test: same direction means inelastic, opposite means elastic.

options.text: price inelastic
options.why: Correct. Price and total revenue moved in the same direction.

questions.explanation: Price fell and total revenue fell. Same-direction movements mean quantity changed by a smaller percentage than price: inelastic.

questions.stem: Compared with a perfectly competitive labor market, a monopsony employer hires

options.text: the same number of workers at the same wage
options.why: Monopsony power changes both employment and the wage.

options.text: more workers at a lower wage
options.why: Because MFC exceeds the wage, the monopsonist restricts hiring.

options.text: fewer workers at a higher wage
options.why: Restricting hiring lets the monopsonist pay a lower wage, read from the supply curve.

options.text: fewer workers at a lower wage
options.why: Correct. It hires where MRP = MFC, with MFC above the supply curve, then pays the wage on the supply curve.

questions.explanation: A monopsonist's MFC lies above labor supply, so MRP = MFC at a lower employment level, and the wage needed to attract those workers is also lower.

questions.stem: Which good is likely to have the most price-elastic demand?

options.text: One particular brand of bottled water
options.why: Correct. Availability of substitutes, necessity, budget share, time and production flexibility drive elasticity.

options.text: Electricity for home heating in the short run
options.why: This good has fewer substitutes or less flexible production, so its quantity responds less to price.

options.text: Table salt
options.why: This good has fewer substitutes or less flexible production, so its quantity responds less to price.

options.text: Insulin for diabetics
options.why: This good has fewer substitutes or less flexible production, so its quantity responds less to price.

questions.explanation: Demand is more elastic with close substitutes, for luxuries, for large budget shares and over longer time periods. Supply is more elastic when production can expand easily.

questions.stem: A firm can sell 8 units at a price of 26 each, or 9 units at a price of 22 each. What is the marginal revenue of unit 9?

options.why: Price exceeds marginal revenue because the price cut applies to all units.
This is total revenue.
This is the price cut, not the change in revenue.
Correct. 198 − 208.

questions.explanation: TR(8) = 208; TR(9) = 198. MR = -10 (negative: demand is inelastic here).

questions.stem: Many workers in the economy become unemployed during a recession. Which of the following best describes the effect on the economy's production possibilities curve (PPC)?

options.text: The economy moves along its PPC.
options.why: Ask whether the economy's resources or technology changed (a shift) or only how fully or for what the resources are used (a movement).

options.text: The PPC shifts outward.
options.why: Ask whether the economy's resources or technology changed (a shift) or only how fully or for what the resources are used (a movement).

options.text: The economy moves to a point inside its PPC.
options.why: Correct. This matches whether resources, technology or only their use has changed.

options.text: The PPC shifts inward.
options.why: Ask whether the economy's resources or technology changed (a shift) or only how fully or for what the resources are used (a movement).

questions.explanation: Changes in the quantity or quality of resources or in technology shift the PPC. Unemployment moves the economy inside the curve; reallocating fully employed resources moves it along the curve.

questions.stem: A country's Lorenz curve moves farther from the line of perfect equality. Which of the following is true?

options.text: The Lorenz curve and the Gini coefficient do not change.
options.why: Think about how the shares of income held by each group change.

options.text: Income inequality increases and the Gini coefficient rises.
options.why: Correct. The Lorenz curve and Gini coefficient measure relative shares, not income levels.

options.text: The Lorenz curve moves toward the line of equality and the Gini coefficient falls.
options.why: Think about how the shares of income held by each group change.

options.text: The Gini coefficient becomes negative.
options.why: The Gini coefficient lies between 0 and 1.

questions.explanation: The farther the Lorenz curve from the 45-degree line, the higher the Gini coefficient and the greater the inequality. Equal proportional changes in all incomes leave shares unchanged.

This subtracts only the implicit cost.

questions.stem: A factory releases pollution into a river used by a downstream town. Which of the following is true?

options.text: The market produces too little; a per-unit subsidy could correct it.
options.why: Decide whether third parties bear a cost (negative) or receive a benefit (positive).

options.text: The market produces the efficient quantity, so no policy is needed.
options.why: Decide whether third parties bear a cost (negative) or receive a benefit (positive).

options.text: The market produces too much; a per-unit subsidy could correct it.
options.why: Decide whether third parties bear a cost (negative) or receive a benefit (positive).

options.text: The market produces too much; a per-unit tax could correct it.
options.why: Correct. Negative externalities cause overproduction; positive ones cause underproduction.

questions.explanation: With a negative externality MSC > MPC and the market overproduces; a Pigouvian tax fixes it. With a positive externality MSB > MPB and the market underproduces; a subsidy fixes it.

questions.stem: A household earning 40,000 pays 6,000 in tax, and a household earning 120,000 pays 13,200. The tax is

options.text: progressive
options.why: Compare the tax as a percentage of income, not the amount paid.

options.text: lump-sum
options.why: A lump-sum tax is the same amount for everyone.

options.text: proportional
options.why: Compare the tax as a percentage of income, not the amount paid.

options.text: regressive
options.why: Correct. The rates are 15% and 11%.

questions.explanation: Tax as a share of income: 15% for the lower income and 11% for the higher. Rising share: progressive; falling: regressive; equal: proportional.

options.text: an inferior good

questions.stem: In a competitive labor market, workers' productivity rises because of better training. Which of the following is most likely?

options.text: Labor supply increases; the wage falls and employment rises.
options.why: Check which curve the event shifts and read the new wage and employment.

options.text: Labor demand increases; the wage and employment rise.
options.why: Correct. Identify whether firms' MRP (demand) or workers' availability (supply) changed.

options.text: Labor supply decreases; the wage rises and employment falls.
options.why: Check which curve the event shifts and read the new wage and employment.

options.text: Labor supply increases; the wage and employment fall.
options.why: Check which curve the event shifts and read the new wage and employment.

questions.explanation: Labor demand depends on MRP (product price and productivity). Labor supply depends on the number of available workers and entry requirements.

questions.stem: Moving from option B to option C, what is the opportunity cost of each additional unit of computers?

options.text: $$\frac{5}{2}$$ units of cars
options.why: This inverts the ratio: it is computers per unit of cars.

options.text: $$\frac{3}{2}$$ units of cars
options.why: This divides the total cars at the first option instead of the amount given up.

options.text: $$\frac{11}{20}$$ units of cars
options.why: This divides totals at the new option; opportunity cost uses the changes.

options.text: $$\frac{2}{5}$$ units of cars
options.why: Correct. 4 units of cars are given up for 10 more units of computers.

questions.explanation: Opportunity cost per unit of computers = (cars given up) ÷ (computers gained) = 4 ÷ 10 = $$\frac{2}{5}$$. The cost rises along the table, so opportunity cost is increasing.

questions.stem: Before a tax, the market price is 23 and quantity is 130. After a per-unit tax of 3, buyers pay 25, sellers keep 22, and quantity falls to 60. What is the deadweight loss?

options.why: Correct. $$\frac{1}{2} \times (130 - 60) \times 3$$.
This is the tax revenue.
The deadweight loss is a triangle: multiply by one half.
The height of the triangle is the whole tax, not the buyers' share.

questions.explanation: DWL = ½ × (lost quantity) × (tax) = ½ × 70 × 3 = 105.

questions.stem: What is the marginal product of worker 6?

options.why: Correct. 64 − 60.
This is total product, not the change in it.
This is the marginal product of the previous worker.
This is average product.

questions.explanation: Marginal product = change in total product = 64 − 60 = 4. Diminishing marginal returns begin after worker 2, where MP starts falling.

questions.stem: How many units should a rational decision-maker choose?

options.why: Stopping here leaves units whose benefit exceeds their cost.
Stopping here leaves units whose benefit exceeds their cost.

This unit costs more than it is worth.

questions.explanation: Keep going while marginal benefit is at least marginal cost. That holds through unit 4 (MB 42, MC 33), but not for the next unit.

questions.stem: Which market structure is described? In long-run equilibrium, price equals average total cost but exceeds marginal cost, and firms have excess capacity.

options.text: Perfect competition
options.why: Recall each structure's number of firms, entry conditions and long-run efficiency.

options.text: Monopoly
options.why: Recall each structure's number of firms, entry conditions and long-run efficiency.

options.text: Monopolistic competition
options.why: Correct. This matches the structure's long-run conditions.

options.text: Oligopoly
options.why: Recall each structure's number of firms, entry conditions and long-run efficiency.

questions.explanation: Perfect competition: P = MC = min ATC. Monopolistic competition: P = ATC > MC, excess capacity. Oligopoly: few interdependent firms. Monopoly: one firm, barriers, possible long-run profit.

questions.stem: What is the marginal product of worker 6?

options.why: Correct. 45 − 44.
This is the marginal product of the previous worker.
This is total product, not the change in it.
This is average product.

questions.explanation: Marginal product = change in total product = 45 − 44 = 1. Diminishing marginal returns begin after worker 2, where MP starts falling.

questions.stem: A firm uses labor (wage 17) and capital (rental price 19). The marginal product of labor is 85 and the marginal product of capital is 114. To produce its output at the lowest cost, the firm should

options.text: keep its input mix unchanged
options.why: The marginal products per dollar are unequal, so costs can be lowered.

options.text: use more of both inputs
options.why: To minimize cost for a given output, shift spending between inputs rather than adding both.

options.text: use more capital and less of the other input
options.why: Correct. Labor yields 5 units per dollar; capital yields 6.

options.text: use more labor and less of the other input
options.why: Compare marginal product per dollar, not marginal product alone.

questions.explanation: MP per dollar: labor 85 ÷ 17 = 5; capital 114 ÷ 19 = 6. Shift toward capital until the ratios are equal.

questions.stem: Which outcome is the Nash equilibrium?

options.text: Firm A does not advertise, Firm B advertises
options.why: At least one firm would switch strategies from this cell to increase its own payoff.

options.text: Firm A does not advertise, Firm B does not advertise
options.why: Correct. Neither firm can raise its own payoff by changing only its own strategy.

options.text: Firm A advertises, Firm B does not advertise
options.why: At least one firm would switch strategies from this cell to increase its own payoff.

options.text: Firm A advertises, Firm B advertises
options.why: At least one firm would switch strategies from this cell to increase its own payoff.

questions.explanation: Check each cell: in (Don't advertise, Don't advertise) with payoffs (8, 7), Firm A would get 6 by switching and Firm B 4, both lower. No other cell has that property.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true?

options.text: Country X has a comparative advantage in bicycles, and Country Y in chairs.
options.why: This reverses the comparison of opportunity costs.

options.text: Country Y has a comparative advantage in bicycles, and Country X in chairs.
options.why: Correct. One unit of bicycles costs 1.25 chairs in X and 1.11 chairs in Y.

options.text: Neither country can gain from trade.
options.why: Different opportunity costs always allow mutually beneficial trade.

options.text: Country X has a comparative advantage in both goods.
options.why: No country can have a comparative advantage in both goods; opportunity costs are reciprocals.

questions.explanation: Compare opportunity costs, not output levels. In X, one bicycles costs $$\frac{5}{4}$$ chairs; in Y, $$\frac{10}{9}$$ chairs. The country with the lower cost has the comparative advantage in bicycles; the other has it in chairs.

questions.stem: A perfectly competitive firm's minimum average variable cost is 28 and its minimum average total cost is 35. The market price is 25. What should the firm do?

options.text: Produce in the short run at a loss; in the long run, firms exit the industry.
options.why: Compare price with minimum AVC (short-run shutdown) and minimum ATC (long-run entry or exit).

options.text: Produce in the short run; it earns an economic profit, so firms enter in the long run.
options.why: Compare price with minimum AVC (short-run shutdown) and minimum ATC (long-run entry or exit).

options.text: Shut down in the short run; in the long run, firms exit the industry.
options.why: Correct. Price is below minimum AVC.

options.text: Shut down in the short run; in the long run, firms enter the industry.
options.why: Firms do not enter an industry that is making losses.

questions.explanation: Short run: produce if P ≥ min AVC (28). Long run: entry if P > min ATC (35), exit if P < min ATC. Here P = 25.

questions.stem: At the world price of 6, domestic consumers buy 96 units and domestic producers supply 20. A tariff of 2 raises the domestic price to 8, where consumers buy 86 and producers supply 31. By how much do imports fall?

options.why: Correct. Imports fall from 76 to 55.
This is only the fall in consumption; domestic production also rises.
This is the level of imports after the tariff.
This is the level of imports before the tariff.

questions.explanation: Imports = domestic quantity demanded − domestic quantity supplied: 76 before, 55 after, a fall of 21.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true about Firm A?

options.text: Firm A has no dominant strategy.
options.why: Compare Firm A's own payoffs (the first number) for each of Firm B's choices.

options.text: Firm A's dominant strategy is to advertise.
options.why: Correct. If B advertises, A gets 6 (advertise) or 1 (not); if B does not, A gets 11 or 4.

options.text: Firm A's dominant strategy is not to advertise.
options.why: Compare Firm A's own payoffs (the first number) for each of Firm B's choices.

options.text: Firm A's dominant strategy depends on Firm B's dominant strategy.
options.why: A dominant strategy, by definition, is best whatever the other firm does.

questions.explanation: A strategy is dominant if it gives the higher payoff whichever strategy the other firm picks. Compare only Firm A's payoffs within each column.

questions.stem: A regulator sets the price a natural monopoly may charge at the level where the demand curve intersects marginal cost. Which of the following results?

options.text: The allocatively efficient quantity is produced, but the firm may need a subsidy because price is below average total cost.
options.why: Correct. At P = MC, output is efficient, but a natural monopoly's ATC exceeds MC.

options.text: Output falls below the unregulated monopoly level.
options.why: A price ceiling below the monopoly price raises output.

options.text: The firm earns zero economic profit.
options.why: With falling ATC above MC, pricing at MC causes a loss.

options.text: The firm earns larger profits than without regulation.
options.why: Regulation lowers the price the firm can charge.

questions.explanation: The socially optimal price (P = MC) gives the efficient quantity but, for a natural monopoly, a loss. The fair-return price (P = ATC) gives zero economic profit with output between the monopoly and efficient levels.

questions.stem: The price of raw materials used in each unit falls. How are the firm's short-run cost curves affected?

options.text: ATC and AFC shift up; MC and AVC do not change.
options.why: Decide whether the change is a fixed cost (does not vary with output) or a variable cost.

options.why: Decide whether the change is a fixed cost (does not vary with output) or a variable cost.

options.text: MC, AVC and ATC all shift down.
options.why: Correct. Fixed costs affect only average fixed and total costs; variable costs affect marginal and average variable costs too.

options.text: MC, AVC and ATC all shift up.
options.why: Decide whether the change is a fixed cost (does not vary with output) or a variable cost.

questions.explanation: A change in fixed cost shifts AFC and ATC but leaves MC and AVC unchanged. A change in a per-unit (variable) cost shifts MC, AVC and ATC.

questions.stem: The government imposes a per-unit tax on a profit-maximizing monopolist. In the short run, what happens to the monopolist's output and price?

options.text: Output falls and price rises.
options.why: Correct. A per-unit tax raises marginal cost.

options.text: Output and price do not change; profit falls.
options.why: A per-unit tax shifts MC up, so the MR = MC quantity falls.

options.text: Output rises and price falls.
options.why: Taxes do not lower the monopolist's costs.

options.text: The monopolist passes the full tax on to consumers with no change in output.
options.why: Output depends on where MR equals MC.

questions.explanation: A per-unit tax raises MC; MR = MC at a lower quantity, and the price read from demand is higher.

questions.stem: A theater charges students less than adults for the same show. Which is most likely true?

options.text: Students' demand is less price elastic than adults' demand.

questions.explanation: Price discrimination needs market power, separable groups and no resale. The less elastic group pays more. Perfect price discrimination produces the efficient quantity with no consumer surplus.

questions.stem: When the price of a good rises from 20 to 22, the quantity demanded falls from 360 to 270. Using the midpoint method, what is the price elasticity of demand, and is demand elastic or inelastic?

questions.explanation: %ΔQ = 90 ÷ 315 ≈ 28.6%; %ΔP = 2 ÷ 21 ≈ 9.5%. Elasticity ≈ 3.00, so demand is elastic.

questions.stem: Which market structure is described? A single firm with high barriers to entry can earn economic profit in the long run.

options.text: Oligopoly
options.why: Recall each structure's number of firms, entry conditions and long-run efficiency.

options.text: Monopolistic competition
options.why: Recall each structure's number of firms, entry conditions and long-run efficiency.

options.text: Monopoly
options.why: Correct. This matches the structure's long-run conditions.

options.text: Perfect competition
options.why: Recall each structure's number of firms, entry conditions and long-run efficiency.

questions.explanation: Perfect competition: P = MC = min ATC. Monopolistic competition: P = ATC > MC, excess capacity. Oligopoly: few interdependent firms. Monopoly: one firm, barriers, possible long-run profit.

questions.stem: A perfectly competitive firm's minimum average variable cost is 11 and its minimum average total cost is 18. The market price is 24. What should the firm do?

options.text: Shut down in the short run; in the long run, firms enter the industry.
options.why: Firms do not enter an industry that is making losses.

options.text: Shut down in the short run; in the long run, firms exit the industry.
options.why: Compare price with minimum AVC (short-run shutdown) and minimum ATC (long-run entry or exit).

options.text: Produce in the short run at a loss; in the long run, firms exit the industry.
options.why: Compare price with minimum AVC (short-run shutdown) and minimum ATC (long-run entry or exit).

options.text: Produce in the short run; it earns an economic profit, so firms enter in the long run.
options.why: Correct. Price is above minimum ATC.

questions.explanation: Short run: produce if P ≥ min AVC (11). Long run: entry if P > min ATC (18), exit if P < min ATC. Here P = 24.

questions.stem: Producing each unit of a good imposes a constant external cost of 14 on third parties. Market demand is $$P = 117 - Q$$ and market supply (marginal private cost) is $$P = 8 + Q$$. What per-unit tax would achieve the socially efficient quantity?

options.why: This is the market quantity, not a tax.

options.text: 0, because the market is already efficient
options.why: With a negative externality, the market overproduces.
The tax should equal the whole external cost per unit.
Correct. A Pigouvian tax equal to the marginal external cost.

questions.explanation: Setting the tax equal to the marginal external cost (14) makes producers face the full social cost, so output falls from 54.5 to 47.5.

questions.stem: In a competitive market, demand increases and, at the same time, supply increases. Which of the following describes the change in equilibrium?

options.text: Price will increase; quantity cannot be determined
options.why: Not this one: Price is indeterminate here, because the two effects work in opposite directions, and quantity will increase.

options.text: Price cannot be determined; quantity will increase
options.why: Correct. Shift each curve separately: one variable moves the same way in both cases, the other depends on the sizes of the shifts.

options.text: Price will increase; quantity will increase
options.why: Not this one: Price is indeterminate here, because the two effects work in opposite directions.

options.text: Price will decrease; quantity will decrease
options.why: Not this one: Price is indeterminate here, because the two effects work in opposite directions, and quantity will increase.

questions.explanation: The demand shift alone moves price up and quantity up. The supply shift alone moves price down and quantity up. Where the effects agree the result is certain; where they conflict it is indeterminate.

questions.stem: A perfectly competitive firm's minimum average variable cost is 22 and its minimum average total cost is 28. The market price is 29. What should the firm do?

options.text: Shut down in the short run; in the long run, firms exit the industry.
options.why: Compare price with minimum AVC (short-run shutdown) and minimum ATC (long-run entry or exit).

options.text: Produce in the short run at a loss; in the long run, firms exit the industry.
options.why: Compare price with minimum AVC (short-run shutdown) and minimum ATC (long-run entry or exit).

options.text: Produce in the short run; it earns an economic profit, so firms enter in the long run.
options.why: Correct. Price is above minimum ATC.

options.text: Shut down in the short run; in the long run, firms enter the industry.
options.why: Firms do not enter an industry that is making losses.

questions.explanation: Short run: produce if P ≥ min AVC (22). Long run: entry if P > min ATC (28), exit if P < min ATC. Here P = 29.

questions.stem: A perfectly competitive, constant-cost industry is in long-run equilibrium. Market demand then decreases permanently. Which of the following describes the long-run adjustment?

options.text: Firms enter, market supply increases, and the price falls further.
options.why: The direction of entry or exit is reversed.

options.text: Firms exit, market supply decreases, and the price rises back to minimum ATC.
options.why: Correct. Short-run losses cause exit.

options.text: Each firm's demand curve becomes downward sloping.
options.why: Firms in perfect competition remain price takers.

options.text: The price stays permanently lower, and firms keep making losses.
options.why: Free entry and exit eliminate economic profit and losses in the long run.

questions.explanation: The lower price creates economic losses. Firms exit, shifting market supply left until price returns to minimum ATC and economic profit is zero.

questions.stem: Demand is $$Q_d = 81 - 2P$$ and supply is $$Q_s = -27 + 4P$$. The government sets a price floor of 20. What results?

options.text: A surplus of 4 units
options.why: Compare quantity demanded with quantity supplied at the controlled price, not with the old equilibrium.

options.text: A shortage of 12 units
options.why: A binding floor (above equilibrium) creates a surplus.

options.text: No effect, because the control is not binding
options.why: Equilibrium price is 18, so a floor of 20 is binding.

options.text: A surplus of 12 units
options.why: Correct. At 20, $$Q_d = 41$$ and $$Q_s = 53$$.

questions.explanation: Equilibrium is P = 18, Q = 45. At the floor of 20, quantity demanded is 41 and quantity supplied is 53: a surplus of 12.

questions.stem: A consumer spends her whole budget on goods A and B. For the last units bought, the marginal utility of A is 6 with a price of 1, and the marginal utility of B is 60 with a price of 6. To maximize utility, she should

options.text: buy more of good A and less of the other good
options.why: Compare marginal utility per dollar, not marginal utility alone.

options.text: buy more of good B and less of the other good
options.why: Correct. Good A gives 6 utils per dollar; good B gives 10.

options.text: buy more of the good with the higher marginal utility, B
options.why: A higher marginal utility does not mean a better buy if the price is also higher.

options.text: keep her purchases unchanged
options.why: The marginal utilities per dollar are not equal, so a better bundle exists.

questions.explanation: MU per dollar: A = 6 ÷ 1 = 6; B = 60 ÷ 6 = 10. Shift spending toward B until the ratios are equal.

questions.stem: A monopsonist can hire 5 workers at a wage of 20 each, or 6 workers at a wage of 21 each. What is the marginal factor cost of worker 6?

options.why: MFC exceeds the wage because the higher wage is paid to all workers.
This is total labor cost.
This is only the raise for one worker.
Correct. 126 − 100.

questions.explanation: Total cost rises from 100 to 126, so MFC = 26, greater than the wage of 21.

questions.stem: In a market with straight-line supply and demand, the equilibrium price is 27 and the equilibrium quantity is 40. The demand curve meets the price axis at 56, and the supply curve meets it at 4. What is consumer surplus?

options.why: This is producer surplus.
Surplus is a triangle: multiply by one half.
This is total surplus.

questions.explanation: Consumer surplus is the triangle below demand and above price: ½ × 40 × (56 − 27) = 580.

questions.stem: How many units should the firm produce to maximize profit?

options.why: Producing more adds units whose marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost.
Producing more adds units whose marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost.
Correct. Unit 3 is the last one whose marginal cost (18) is at most the price (MR) of 22.
This unit costs more than the price it sells for.

questions.explanation: For a price taker, MR = P = 22. Produce every unit whose MC is at most 22: units 1 to 3.

questions.stem: A monopolist faces demand $$P = 45 - Q$$ and has constant marginal cost and average total cost of 19. What is the profit-maximizing quantity?

options.why: This is the efficient quantity where P = MC.
MR = MC sets the quantity; MR has twice the slope of demand.
This is where demand reaches a price of zero.

questions.explanation: MR = 45 − 2Q. Setting MR = MC: Q = 13; price from demand: P = 32. Profit = (32 − 19) × 13 = 169. The efficient quantity is 26, so DWL = ½ × 13 × 13 = 84.5.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true about Firm A?

options.text: Firm A's dominant strategy is not to advertise.
options.why: Correct. If B advertises, A gets 3 (advertise) or 5 (not); if B does not, A gets 1 or 10.

options.text: Firm A has no dominant strategy.
options.why: Compare Firm A's own payoffs (the first number) for each of Firm B's choices.

options.text: Firm A's dominant strategy depends on Firm B's dominant strategy.
options.why: A dominant strategy, by definition, is best whatever the other firm does.

options.text: Firm A's dominant strategy is to advertise.
options.why: Compare Firm A's own payoffs (the first number) for each of Firm B's choices.

questions.explanation: A strategy is dominant if it gives the higher payoff whichever strategy the other firm picks. Compare only Firm A's payoffs within each column.
